topics.title: Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
topics.summary: Normal stool is soft, formed, brown, and about 75% water. When movement through the bowel speeds up, slows down, or stops, you get diarrhea, constipation, or obstruction, and each one carries its own dangers.
objectives: After this lesson you can describe normal feces.
List the factors that affect bowel elimination and explain how several of them work.
Compare diarrhea, flatulence, constipation, and bowel (fecal) incontinence: what each one is, what causes it, and what it puts the client at risk for.
Explain the difference between diverticulosis and diverticulitis and name the complications of diverticulitis.
Tell a mechanical bowel obstruction from a functional one, and explain why a paralytic ileus is dangerous.
topics.bigPicture:
Elimination is how the body gets rid of its wastes. Bowel elimination removes the unused portions of solid material we eat, whatever the body could not digest or absorb.

Picture the intestines as a conveyor belt running through a sponge. As the belt carries waste along, the sponge (the wall of the large intestine) soaks up water. Speed is everything. If the belt runs too fast, there is no time to absorb water, and stool comes out liquid (diarrhea). If it runs too slow, too much water is pulled out, and stool turns hard and dry (constipation). If the belt stops, whether something is blocking it or the motor has quit, you have a bowel obstruction, and that is an emergency.

keyTerms.def: Solid waste passed from the bowel. Normally about 75% water and 25% solid material.
Wave-like muscle contractions that push contents forward through the digestive tract.
Passage of liquid feces with increased frequency.
Excessive gas in the intestines or colon.
Fewer than three bowel movements per week, or difficulty passing stools that may be hard and dry.
Inability to voluntarily control the passing of feces and intestinal gas through the anal sphincter.
Small outpouchings of the colon wall, formed when the mucosal lining herniates (pushes) through the bowel wall. One pouch is a diverticulum.
Inflammation of the diverticula. It can cause obstruction, perforation, and bleeding.
Inability of intestinal contents to move through the small or large bowel.
A functional obstruction in which the intestinal muscles become adynamic (stop moving), often after surgery or certain drugs.

sections.heading: A quick trip through the bowel
sections.body:
After food leaves the stomach as chyme, it enters the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed. What is left moves into the large intestine (colon). The colon's main job is to absorb water and electrolytes and store waste until it can be passed. The longer stool sits in the colon, the more water is removed and the harder it gets.

Contents are pushed along by peristalsis, waves of muscle contraction. When stool reaches the rectum, the rectal wall stretches and the person feels the urge to defecate. Two rings of muscle guard the exit: the internal anal sphincter, which is involuntary (it works automatically), and the external anal sphincter, which is voluntary. Because we control the external sphincter, we can delay a bowel movement until we reach a toilet.

Eating also gets the bowel moving. Food entering the stomach triggers the gastrocolic reflex, a strong wave of movement in the colon, so many people feel the urge to have a bowel movement after a meal, often after breakfast. You will use this reflex later when you plan bowel training.

check.q: Why does stool become harder the longer it stays in the colon?
check.a: The colon keeps absorbing water from it. More time means more water removed, so the stool turns hard and dry.

sections.heading: What normal feces look like
sections.body: Your slides describe normal feces as about 75% water and 25% solid material. The solid part includes bile, intestinal secretions, shed epithelial cells (cells that line the gut and are constantly replaced), bacteria, and inorganic material such as calcium and phosphate. Small amounts of seeds, meat fiber, and fat may also be present, and that is still normal.
bullets: Soft but formed: holds a shape but is easy to pass.
Requires normal fluid intake: if the client is not drinking enough, the colon pulls more water from stool and it hardens.
Brown: the color comes from bile pigments broken down by gut bacteria. A big color change (black, red, clay-colored) is a clue that something is wrong. You will learn those in the assessment lesson.
Flatus: the intestines produce about 7–10 L of gas every 24 hours. Most of it is absorbed or moves along without the person noticing; only part of it is passed.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client is worried about seeds in a soft, formed, brown stool. Reassure them: small amounts of seeds or fiber are normal.

sections.heading: Factors that affect bowel elimination
sections.body: Your slides list ten factors that change how fast the bowel runs. When a pattern changes, run through this list.

table.caption: Factors affecting bowel elimination (from your slides)
rows: Diet
Fiber adds bulk and holds water, keeping stool soft. Low fiber slows the bowel; some foods cause gas or diarrhea.
Fluid
Too little fluid means harder, drier stool.
Activity
Movement stimulates peristalsis; immobility slows it.
Defecation habits
Ignoring the urge lets stool dry out and harden. Lack of privacy or a changed routine makes people hold it.
Medications
Opioids and iron constipate; antibiotics can cause diarrhea; laxatives speed the bowel up.
Diagnostic procedures
NPO status and bowel preps empty the bowel; barium can harden afterward.
Anesthesia and surgical procedures
Slow or temporarily stop peristalsis.
Pathologic conditions
Bowel diseases or nerve damage (such as spinal cord injury) change motility and control.
Pain
Hemorrhoids, an incision, or a perineal tear make the person delay defecation.
Psychologic factors
Stress can speed the bowel up; depression can slow it down.

check.q: A post-op client is on bed rest, receiving opioids for pain, and has been NPO. How many bowel risk factors can you find?
check.a: At least four: reduced activity, medications (opioids), low fluid/food intake, and anesthesia/surgery. All of them slow the bowel, so this client is at high risk for constipation.

sections.heading: Diarrhea: the belt runs too fast
sections.body: Diarrhea is the passage of liquid feces with increased frequency. Contents rush through too fast for the colon to absorb water.
bullets: The urge to defecate is difficult or impossible to control. Clients with diarrhea may not make it to the bathroom, so keep the call light, bedpan, or commode within reach and answer quickly.
Cramps and more frequent bowel sounds: the hyperactive bowel is moving hard and often.

Fluid and electrolyte losses: water, sodium, and potassium leave with the stool. Infants and older adults become dehydrated fastest. Monitor intake and output, daily weights, and signs of dehydration.
Risk for skin breakdown: liquid stool contains digestive enzymes and acids that irritate the perianal skin. Cleanse gently after each stool, pat dry, and apply a moisture barrier.
sections.example: At the bedside: An 82-year-old client has had six watery stools since morning. Check for dehydration (dry mouth, low urine output, dizziness on standing), keep an accurate I&O, protect the perianal skin, keep the commode close, and report the stool frequency to the provider.

sections.heading: Flatulence: too much gas
sections.body: Flatulence means excessive gas in the intestines or colon. It causes bloating, cramping, and belching. Your slides list five causes:
bullets: Bacterial action on chyme: gut bacteria ferment food and give off gas.
Swallowed air: eating fast, chewing gum, drinking through a straw, carbonated drinks, and anxious rapid breathing all add air.
Gas diffusing from the bloodstream into the intestine.
Foods: beans, cabbage, onions, cauliflower, and other gas-forming foods.
Abdominal surgery: peristalsis slows after surgery, so gas builds up. Walking as allowed helps move it along.

sections.heading: Constipation: the belt runs too slow
sections.body:
Your slides define constipation as the passage of fewer than three bowel movements per week, or difficulty passing stools, which may be hard and dry. Notice the word or: a client who goes every day but strains to pass hard, painful stool is still constipated.

The main cause is decreased motility, meaning the bowel moves contents slowly, so the colon has extra time to pull water out. Constipation may reflect a primary problem, such as too little fiber, too little fluid, inactivity, or ignoring the urge. Or it may be a sign of an underlying disorder, such as a nerve problem or something blocking the bowel. That is why a new or lasting change always deserves a closer look.

Always compare with the client's own usual pattern. Untreated, hard stool can build into a fecal impaction, which the exemplar lesson covers in depth. One clue to know now: a client with an impaction may pass small amounts of liquid stool that seeps around the hard mass. It looks like diarrhea, but the real problem is a blockage of hard stool.

check.q: A client has a bowel movement daily but says, "I have to push really hard and the stool is like little rocks." Is this constipation?
check.a: Yes. Constipation is fewer than three BMs a week OR difficulty passing stools that may be hard and dry. Frequency alone does not rule it out.

sections.heading: Bowel (fecal) incontinence
sections.body:
Bowel incontinence (also called fecal incontinence) is the inability to voluntarily control the passing of feces and intestinal gas through the anal sphincter. Controlling the bowel takes three things: feeling that the rectum is full, a strong sphincter to hold stool, and a brain that can respond. A problem with any of them can cause incontinence.

Your slides stress that it is usually a manifestation of another disorder, not a disease by itself. Causes include:
bullets: Neurologic disorders: stroke, spinal cord injury, and dementia interfere with sensation or control.
Depression can reduce a person's motivation or ability to respond to the urge.
Traumatic injuries, such as damage to the sphincter during childbirth.
Inflammatory processes or masses in the bowel.
Hemorrhoids or a deformity of the anus that keeps the sphincter from closing completely.

check.q: Why do your slides call fecal incontinence a "manifestation" rather than a disease?
check.a: Because it is usually a sign of another disorder (neurologic, traumatic, inflammatory, and so on). The nurse protects the skin and helps find the cause.

sections.heading: Diverticular disease
sections.body:
Diverticular disease involves outpouchings of the colon. The mucosal lining of the bowel herniates (pushes out) through weak spots in the bowel wall, forming small pouches called diverticula. Simply having these pouches is called diverticulosis, and many people have them without symptoms. A low-fiber diet and the straining that comes with it are commonly linked to their development.

Trouble starts when the pouches become inflamed, usually because stool or bacteria get trapped inside. That is diverticulitis. Clients often have abdominal pain (commonly in the lower left abdomen, where the sigmoid colon is), fever, and changes in bowel habits. Your slides list its three serious complications:
bullets: Obstruction: swelling and scarring can narrow or block the colon.
Perforation: an inflamed pouch can rupture and spill bowel contents into the abdomen, causing a serious infection of the abdominal lining (peritonitis).
Bleeding: blood vessels near the pouches can bleed, so the client may pass blood rectally.
sections.analogy: Think of an old bicycle tire with an inner tube. Where the tire wall is thin, the inner tube bulges out in little bubbles. That is diverticulosis. If a bubble gets irritated and swollen, it can block the tube, burst, or bleed. That is diverticulitis.

check.q: What is the difference between diverticulosis and diverticulitis?
check.a: Diverticulosis means the outpouchings are present, often with no symptoms. Diverticulitis means they are inflamed, which can lead to obstruction, perforation, and bleeding.

sections.heading: Bowel obstruction: the belt stops
sections.body: A bowel obstruction is the inability of intestinal contents to move through the small or large bowel. There are two main kinds, and the difference is why things stopped moving.

table.caption: Two kinds of bowel obstruction
rows: Mechanical
Something physically blocks the bowel. The muscle may be working hard, but contents can't get past the blockage.

Adhesions (bands of scar tissue, often after surgery); hernias (a loop of bowel trapped in a weak spot); intussusception (one part of the bowel telescopes into the next); volvulus (the bowel twists on itself); tumors
Functional
The bowel is open, but peristalsis can't push contents forward. The motor has stopped.
Paralytic ileus: the intestinal muscles are adynamic (not moving). It often occurs after surgery or drugs such as anesthesia and opioids.

steps: Contents stop moving, so fluid, gas, and stool build up behind the obstruction.
The bowel stretches. The client develops abdominal distention, cramping pain, nausea and vomiting, and stops passing stool and flatus.
Pressure inside the swollen bowel squeezes its own blood vessels, cutting off blood flow to the bowel wall.
Without blood, bowel tissue dies (bowel necrosis) and can tear open (perforation), spilling contents into the abdomen. Your slides name both as the key risks.
sections.example: At the bedside: Two days after abdominal surgery, a client's abdomen is distended and firm, the client is nauseated and hasn't passed flatus, and you hear no bowel sounds after listening carefully. This points to a paralytic ileus. Report it promptly, keep the client NPO as ordered, and expect orders such as a nasogastric tube. (With a mechanical blockage, bowel sounds are often high-pitched early on; with an ileus, they are hypoactive or absent.)

pearls: Speed sets stool consistency: too fast = liquid (diarrhea), too slow = hard and dry (constipation), stopped = obstruction.
Constipation is fewer than 3 BMs per week OR hard stools that are difficult to pass. A daily BM doesn't rule it out.
Diarrhea brings two big nursing risks: fluid and electrolyte loss, and skin breakdown.
Fecal incontinence is usually a sign of another disorder. Look for the cause.
Diverticulitis (inflamed pouches) can obstruct, perforate, or bleed.
redFlags: Abdominal distention, vomiting, cramping pain, and no stool or flatus → suspect bowel obstruction; report to the provider promptly, keep the client NPO as ordered, and monitor closely.
A client with diverticulitis whose pain suddenly worsens and whose abdomen becomes rigid and board-like, with fever → possible perforation; notify the provider immediately.
Frequent watery stools with dizziness, very low urine output, or confusion, especially in an infant or older adult → serious fluid loss; report and monitor I&O and vital signs.
recap: Normal feces: about 75% water and 25% solids (bile, secretions, shed cells, bacteria, calcium and phosphate); soft, formed, and brown.
Ten factors affect bowel elimination: diet, fluid, activity, habits, medications, diagnostic procedures, anesthesia/surgery, pathologic conditions, pain, and psychologic factors.
Diarrhea: liquid, frequent stools; urge hard to control; cramps and increased bowel sounds; F&E losses; skin breakdown.
Flatulence causes: bacterial action, swallowed air, gas from the bloodstream, foods, abdominal surgery.
Constipation: fewer than 3 BMs per week or difficult hard, dry stools; caused by decreased motility.
Fecal incontinence is usually a manifestation of another disorder.
Diverticulitis = inflamed diverticula → obstruction, perforation, bleeding.
Mechanical obstruction = physical block; functional (paralytic ileus) = peristalsis stops. Both risk necrosis and perforation.

checks.q: Why can a client with diarrhea become dehydrated while a client with constipation has hard stool? Explain using what the colon does.
checks.a: The colon absorbs water. In diarrhea, contents move too fast for water to be absorbed, so water is lost in stool. In constipation, stool sits longer and more water is pulled out, so it becomes hard and dry.

checks.q: Name three mechanical causes of bowel obstruction and the main functional cause.
checks.a: Mechanical: adhesions, hernias, intussusception, volvulus, tumors (any three). Functional: paralytic ileus.

checks.q: A post-op client has a distended abdomen, absent bowel sounds, and no flatus. What do you suspect, and what serious complications are you worried about?
checks.a: Paralytic ileus, a functional obstruction. The risks are bowel necrosis and perforation. Report it promptly.

checks.q: Why does diarrhea redden perianal skin?
checks.a: Liquid stool carries enzymes and acids. Cleanse gently, pat dry, apply a moisture barrier.

topics.title: Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
topics.summary: Bowel assessment starts with the client's story: their pattern, their stool, their aids, diet, medications, and any ostomy. Then comes a physical exam where you listen before you touch, and finally you need to know what each diagnostic test involves for the client.
objectives: After this lesson you can list what to ask in a bowel elimination history, including use of elimination aids and ostomy management.
Explain the difference between a colostomy and an ileostomy and predict stool consistency from the stoma's location.
Describe a healthy stoma and recognize stoma findings that must be reported.
Perform the abdominal exam in the correct order and explain why auscultation comes before palpation.
Describe the stool characteristics to observe and what abnormal findings may mean.
Explain the purpose of, and the key nursing points for, fecal and blood tests, digital rectal exam, colonoscopy, barium enema, colorectal transit study, and EGD.
topics.bigPicture:
Bowel habits are private, and many clients are embarrassed to talk about them. That makes your assessment skills even more important. A good bowel assessment answers three questions: What is normal for this person? What has changed? Why?

You collect that information in three ways: by talking with the client (history), by examining the abdomen, rectum, and stool (physical exam), and by helping with diagnostic tests that let the team see inside the bowel. Many clients you care for will also have an ostomy, a surgically made opening for stool, so you need to know how to assess one.

keyTerms.def: A person's usual frequency, timing, and ease of bowel movements.
Anything a person uses to help have a bowel movement, such as laxatives, enemas, suppositories, prune juice, or a morning coffee routine.
A surgically created opening from an internal organ to the surface of the body. For the bowel, it lets stool leave through the abdominal wall.
The visible end of the bowel that has been brought out through the abdominal wall.
An ostomy made from the colon (large intestine).
An ostomy made from the ileum (the last part of the small intestine).
Black, tarry stool that usually means bleeding high in the GI tract.
Blood in stool that is hidden (not visible) and found only by testing.
A procedure in which a flexible scope with a camera views the inside of the entire colon. Tissue samples can be taken.
A scope passed through the mouth to view the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum.

sections.heading: Start with the client's story
sections.body:
Your slides list what to cover when you observe and interview a client about bowel elimination. Provide privacy, use words the client understands, and stay matter-of-fact. Your comfort helps the client feel comfortable.

Normal frequency varies widely, from several times a day to a few times a week. What matters most is the client's own usual pattern and any change from it.
bullets: Defecation pattern: "How often do you usually have a bowel movement? What time of day?"
Description of feces and any changes: "What does your stool usually look like? Have you noticed any change in color, shape, or how hard or soft it is?"
Fecal elimination problems: diarrhea, constipation, gas, incontinence, pain, or bleeding.
Factors influencing elimination: use of elimination aids (laxatives, enemas, routines), diet, fluid, exercise, medications, and stress.
Presence and management of an ostomy: whether the client has an ileostomy or colostomy, how they care for it, and any problems with the skin, the pouch, or coping.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client says, "I'm fine, I just take a laxative every night." That is an important finding, not a passing comment. Daily laxative use can weaken the bowel's natural reflexes. Ask how long they have used it and what happens when they don't.

sections.heading: Ostomies: colostomy vs ileostomy
sections.body:
An ostomy is a surgically created opening that lets stool leave the body through the abdominal wall instead of the anus. The part you can see is the stoma, the end of the intestine stitched to the skin. Stool collects in a pouch attached to the skin around the stoma. Clients may need an ostomy because of cancer, an obstruction, perforation, inflammatory bowel disease, or trauma. Ostomies can be temporary (to let the bowel heal) or permanent.

The name tells you where the stoma comes from. A colostomy is made from the colon. An ileostomy is made from the ileum, the end of the small intestine. A stoma has no sphincter and no nerve endings for touch or pain, so the client can't control when stool comes out and won't feel it if the stoma is injured.

sections.heading: Location predicts what comes out
sections.body: Remember that the colon absorbs water as stool travels along it. So the farther along the bowel the stoma is, the more water has been removed and the more formed the stool will be.

table.caption: Stoma location and expected output
rows: Ileostomy (small intestine)
Liquid to pasty, drains often and fairly constantly
Contains digestive enzymes that quickly damage skin, so the pouch must fit well. High risk of dehydration and electrolyte loss, so monitor I&O.
Ascending colostomy
Liquid to semi-liquid
Similar to ileostomy: skin protection and fluid balance.
Transverse colostomy
Mushy, semi-formed
Unpredictable timing; a pouch is needed.
Descending colostomy
Semi-formed to formed
More solid, closer to normal stool.
Sigmoid colostomy
Formed
Output may become regular enough that the client can predict it.

sections.analogy: Think of the colon as a long towel wringing out a wet cloth. Cut in near the start (ileostomy, ascending colon) and the cloth is still dripping. Cut in near the end (sigmoid) and it is nearly wrung dry.

check.q: Which client is at greater risk for dehydration and peristomal skin breakdown: one with an ileostomy or one with a sigmoid colostomy? Why?
check.a: The client with an ileostomy. Its output is liquid, frequent, and full of digestive enzymes, because it leaves the bowel before the colon can absorb water.

sections.heading: Assessing the stoma and the skin around it
sections.body:
A healthy stoma is moist and pink to beefy red, like the inside of your mouth, and usually sits slightly above the skin. It has a rich blood supply, so it may bleed slightly when touched or cleaned, which is expected. Right after surgery the stoma is swollen; the swelling goes down over the following weeks, so the stoma is measured often and the pouch opening resized.

A stoma that is pale, dusky (bluish), purple, or black is not getting enough blood. That tissue can die, so report it immediately. Also check:
bullets: Peristomal skin (the skin around the stoma): it should be intact, with no redness, rash, or open areas. Leaking stool quickly damages this skin.
Output: amount, color, consistency, and odor, compared with what you expect for that stoma location.
Pouch fit: any leaks, or an opening cut too large.
The client's coping and self-care: how they feel about the change in their body, and whether they (or a caregiver) can empty and change the pouch.
sections.example: At the bedside: On the morning after colostomy surgery, the stoma looked moist and red. Now you find it dark purple and dry. This is a change in perfusion. Notify the surgeon right away and document what you see.

sections.heading: The abdominal exam: listen before you touch
sections.body: Your slides list the four exam techniques for the abdomen: inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation, with a special focus on the intestinal tract. For most body systems, you inspect, palpate, percuss, then auscultate. The abdomen is different. You auscultate before palpating, because palpation can alter peristalsis. Pressing on the belly can stir up bowel sounds that weren't there, or quiet them, which would give you a false result.
steps: Inspect: look at the shape (flat, rounded, distended), scars, visible movement, and the skin. A distended abdomen with a history of surgery should make you think of adhesions or ileus.

Auscultate: use the diaphragm of the stethoscope in all four quadrants. Normal bowel sounds are irregular clicks and gurgles, roughly 5–30 per minute. Note whether they are hypoactive (few), hyperactive (many and loud, as in diarrhea), or absent. Before you call them absent, listen for several minutes.
Percuss: a drum-like sound (tympany) over gas is common; dullness can suggest stool, fluid, or a mass.
Palpate: light, then deeper, checking for tenderness, firmness, or masses. Palpate any painful area last.
Inspect and palpate the rectum and anus: look for hemorrhoids, fissures (small tears), skin breakdown, or stool leakage.
sections.analogy: It is like checking whether fish are moving in a pond. You watch and listen first. If you throw a rock in before you listen, you can't tell what was happening before you disturbed it.

check.q: Why does the nurse auscultate the abdomen before palpating it?
check.a: Palpation can alter peristalsis, which changes the bowel sounds and gives a false picture of bowel activity.

sections.heading: Observe the stool
sections.body: Your slides list six things to observe about stool: color, consistency, shape, amount, odor, and the presence of abnormal constituents. Knowing the common abnormal findings helps you spot problems early.

table.caption: Stool characteristics
headers: Abnormal and what it may mean
rows: Color
Brown (infants: yellow to tan/green)

Black, tarry (melena): bleeding high in the GI tract; iron supplements can also turn stool black. Red: bleeding low in the GI tract or near the anus (beets can do this too). Clay-colored or white: bile is not reaching the bowel; also seen for a day or two after barium.
Consistency
Soft, formed
Liquid (diarrhea, fast transit); hard and dry (constipation).
Shape
Shaped like the rectum, about 2.5 cm across
Narrow, pencil-shaped stool can mean something is narrowing the bowel, such as a mass.
Amount
Varies with diet
Small amounts of liquid, foul-smelling stool with no formed stool can be liquid seeping around a fecal impaction; it is not true diarrhea.
Odor
Characteristic, affected by diet
Unusually foul odor can come from infection or blood.
Abnormal constituents
Small amounts of seeds, fiber, or fat
Blood, pus, a lot of mucus, parasites, large amounts of fat (greasy, floating stool), or swallowed objects.

sections.example: At the bedside: A client taking an iron supplement has dark, almost black stool. Iron can do this, but black tarry stool can also mean upper GI bleeding. Don't assume. Document it, check the vital signs, and report it so the provider can decide whether to test the stool for blood.

sections.heading: Diagnostic tests and what the nurse does
sections.body: Your slides list the main bowel diagnostic tests. For each one, know what it looks for and how you prepare and monitor the client.

table.caption: Bowel diagnostic tests
rows: Blood tests
For example, a blood count to look for anemia from blood loss, and electrolytes after diarrhea or vomiting
Standard blood draw; review results for low hemoglobin or electrolyte losses.
Fecal tests
Fecal occult blood test (hidden blood, used in colorectal cancer screening); stool culture (bacteria); ova and parasites

Collect stool without mixing in urine or toilet paper; use a clean container or a "hat" in the toilet. Send fresh samples to the lab promptly. Follow any diet or medication instructions for occult blood tests.
Digital rectal exam (DRE)
The provider inserts a gloved, lubricated finger into the rectum

Detects masses, hemorrhoids, impacted stool, and (in men) prostate enlargement. Position the client on their side and provide privacy. Stimulating the rectum can trigger a vagal response (slow heart rate), so watch for dizziness.
Colonoscopy
A flexible scope views the whole colon; tissue samples (biopsies) can be taken and polyps removed

Before: bowel prep (clear liquids and a laxative prep until the output is clear liquid) and consent. After: monitor vital signs as sedation wears off; gas and cramping are expected. Report signs of perforation: severe abdominal pain, abdominal distension, fever, or a rigid abdomen (also heavy rectal bleeding).
X-ray imaging / barium enema
Barium (a contrast liquid) is put into the colon through the rectum, then x-rays outline the bowel
Before: the bowel must be empty. After: encourage fluids and give a laxative as ordered, because barium can harden and cause constipation or impaction. Stool will be white or chalky for a day or two.
Colorectal transit study
The client swallows a capsule containing markers; x-rays over several days show how fast they move through
Used to evaluate constipation and slow motility. The client usually avoids laxatives and enemas during the study so results reflect the bowel's real speed.
EGD
A scope through the mouth views the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum
Before: NPO and consent. The throat is numbed. After: give nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns to prevent aspiration. Report severe pain or bleeding.

check.q: A client returns from an EGD and asks for water. What must you check first?
check.a: That the gag reflex has returned. The throat was numbed, so drinking before the gag reflex is back could cause aspiration.

pearls: In the abdominal exam, inspect → auscultate → percuss → palpate. Palpating first can alter peristalsis.
The farther along the bowel the stoma is, the more formed the stool: ileostomy = liquid, sigmoid colostomy = formed.
A healthy stoma is moist and pink to beefy red. A pale, dusky, purple, or black stoma means poor blood flow: report it immediately.
Ileostomy output is enzyme-rich and liquid. Protect the skin and watch fluid balance.
After barium: fluids and a laxative as ordered; expect white stool for a day or two.
After EGD: nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns.
redFlags: A stoma that turns dusky, purple, or black → not enough blood flow; notify the provider immediately.
Black, tarry stool, especially with dizziness, a rising heart rate, or low blood pressure → possible GI bleeding; check vital signs and report promptly.
After colonoscopy, severe abdominal pain, abdominal distension, fever, or a rigid abdomen → possible perforation; notify the provider immediately (also report heavy rectal bleeding).
recap: History: defecation pattern, description of feces and changes, problems, influencing factors (elimination aids, diet, fluid, exercise, medications, stress), and presence and management of an ostomy.
Ileostomy = from the ileum (liquid, enzyme-rich output); colostomy = from the colon (output gets more formed the farther along it is).
Healthy stoma: moist and pink to beefy red. Pale, dusky, or black is abnormal.
Abdominal exam order: inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation. Auscultation comes before palpation because palpation can alter peristalsis.
Inspect and palpate the rectum and anus.
Observe stool color, consistency, shape, amount, odor, and abnormal constituents.
Diagnostics: blood and fecal tests, DRE, colonoscopy (tissue samples possible), x-ray/barium enema, colorectal transit study, EGD.

checks.q: A client has an ascending colostomy. Will you expect formed or liquid stool, and why?
checks.a: Liquid to semi-liquid. The stoma is early in the colon, so little water has been absorbed yet.

checks.q: List the six stool characteristics your slides tell you to observe.
checks.a: Color, consistency, shape, amount, odor, and presence of abnormal constituents.

checks.q: A client had a barium enema yesterday and has not had a bowel movement. Why is this a concern, and what do you expect to do?
checks.a: Retained barium can harden and cause constipation or impaction. Encourage fluids, give the laxative as ordered, and report if the client still doesn't pass the barium.

checks.q: During a colonoscopy, what can the provider do besides look at the colon?
checks.a: Take tissue samples (biopsies) and remove polyps.

topics.title: Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
topics.summary: Most bowel care is nursing care: fluid, fiber, teaching, bowel training, pelvic floor exercises, hygiene, and ostomy care. Medications and surgery are added when needed. Prevention depends on healthy habits and asking clients directly about symptoms they may be too embarrassed to raise.
objectives: After this lesson you can describe the independent nursing interventions for bowel elimination and explain why each works.
Teach a client a basic bowel training routine that uses the gastrocolic reflex.
Describe basic ostomy care and the teaching an ostomy client needs.
Compare laxatives, stool softeners, and antidiarrheal agents, including key cautions, and name the indications for bowel surgery.
List prevention habits and modifiable risk factors for bowel and bladder problems and explain why each matters.
Explain why screening for elimination problems requires direct questioning.
topics.bigPicture:
Your slides split bowel care into two groups. Independent interventions are things a nurse can start without a provider's order: encouraging fluid and fiber, teaching, bowel training, pelvic floor exercises, hygiene, and ostomy care. Collaborative therapies need the team: medications (laxatives, stool softeners, antidiarrheals) and surgery.

Start with the independent measures. They fix the cause, while medications often only treat the symptom. A client who drinks enough, eats enough fiber, moves around, and answers the urge to go may never need a laxative. The best intervention of all is prevention, and much of prevention is teaching.

keyTerms.def: An action a nurse can start without a provider's order, based on nursing judgment.
Treatment that needs a provider's order or the interprofessional team, such as medications or surgery.
The part of plant foods the body can't digest. It adds bulk and holds water in stool.
A program that sets a regular time and routine for defecation to restore a predictable pattern.
Repeated tightening and relaxing of the pelvic floor muscles to strengthen bowel and bladder control.
A medication that promotes a bowel movement.
A medication that lets water mix into stool so it is softer and easier to pass without straining.
A medication that slows intestinal movement to reduce diarrhea.
A risk factor the person can change or that can be reduced, such as obesity or diet.

sections.heading: Fluid and fiber: the first-line tools
sections.body: The first independent intervention on your slides is encouraging increased intake of fluid and fiber. They work as a team. Fiber adds bulk and holds water in the stool, which keeps it soft, and the bulk stretches the bowel wall and stimulates peristalsis. Fluid gives the fiber water to hold. Fiber without enough fluid can actually make stool harder and cause bloating.
bullets: Fiber sources: whole-grain breads and cereals, fresh fruits, vegetables, beans, and bran. Daily goals in your exemplar are about 25 g for women and 38 g for men.
Increase fiber gradually to limit gas and bloating.
Fluid: unless the client has a fluid restriction, encourage about 2,000 mL or more per day, spread through the day.
Check for restrictions first. A client with heart failure or kidney disease may be on a fluid limit. Follow the provider's orders.

check.q: Why should a client increase fluid at the same time as fiber?
check.a: Fiber works by holding water in stool. Without enough fluid, extra fiber can make stool harder and cause bloating.

sections.heading: Teaching about dietary choices
sections.body: Your slides list teaching about the impact of dietary choices as an independent intervention. Help clients connect what they eat with how their bowel behaves.
bullets: Foods that tend to constipate: low-fiber, highly processed foods; large amounts of cheese and meat.
Foods that loosen stool: fruits (especially prunes), vegetables, whole grains.
Gas-forming foods: beans, cabbage, onions, cauliflower, carbonated drinks.
Irritants: caffeine, alcohol, artificial sweeteners, and spicy or acidic foods can irritate the bowel and bladder.
Food safety: cooking and storing food properly prevents foodborne illness and diarrhea.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client with constipation says, "I eat a big bowl of white rice and chicken every night and drink coffee all day." You can teach swaps: brown rice or whole grains, a vegetable with dinner, fruit for snacks, and water in place of some of the coffee.

sections.heading: Bowel training: building a routine
sections.body: Bowel training sets up a regular, predictable time for bowel movements. It helps clients with chronic constipation, with fecal incontinence, or with nerve problems that affect bowel control. It works because the bowel responds to routine and to the gastrocolic reflex, the wave of colon activity triggered by eating.
steps: Learn the client's usual pattern and choose a consistent time, ideally after a meal (often breakfast) to take advantage of the gastrocolic reflex.
Offer a warm drink with or after the meal; warm liquids can help stimulate the bowel.

At the planned time, help the client onto the toilet or commode, sitting upright with feet supported and leaning slightly forward. This position uses gravity and makes pushing easier. Use a bedpan only if there is no other option.
Provide privacy and enough time. Don't rush the client.
Teach the client never to ignore the urge to defecate.
Repeat at the same time every day, along with adequate fluid, fiber, and activity. It may take weeks to establish a pattern.
sections.analogy: Bowel training is like setting a body clock. If you go to bed at the same time every night, you start feeling sleepy right on schedule. Sit on the toilet after breakfast every day and the bowel learns the schedule too.

sections.heading: Pelvic floor exercises and personal hygiene
sections.body:
Pelvic floor exercises (Kegel exercises) strengthen the muscles that support the rectum and bladder, including the anal sphincter. They help with fecal and urinary incontinence. The client tightens the muscles used to hold back a bowel movement or stop the flow of urine, holds for a few seconds, relaxes, and repeats several times a day. You will learn the exact technique in the incontinence lessons.

Personal hygiene protects skin and prevents infection:
bullets: Clean the perineal area gently after every stool, especially with diarrhea or incontinence, and pat it dry.
Wipe front to back to keep stool bacteria away from the urethra.
Apply a moisture barrier cream when the skin is exposed to stool often.
Hand hygiene after toileting prevents spreading infectious diarrhea to others.

sections.heading: Ostomy care
sections.body: Ostomy care is an independent nursing intervention, and a big part of it is teaching the client to manage at home. Key points:
bullets: Empty the pouch when it is about one-third to one-half full. A heavy pouch can pull loose and leak.
Change the skin barrier on a regular schedule, or sooner if it leaks. Leaking stool damages the skin.
Measure the stoma and cut the barrier opening to fit closely around it, only slightly larger than the stoma, so the skin is covered but the stoma isn't squeezed.
Clean the peristomal skin with warm water, pat it dry, and inspect the stoma and skin with every change.
Teach the client how to empty and change the pouch, which foods cause gas or odor, and (for an ileostomy) to drink enough fluid to replace losses.
Support body image. Many clients grieve the change. Listen, and involve the wound and ostomy nurse.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client with a new ileostomy says the skin around the stoma burns and the pouch keeps leaking. You remove the pouch and find the barrier opening was cut much larger than the stoma, so enzyme-rich stool is touching the skin. Re-measure, cut the opening to fit closely, protect the skin, and ask the wound and ostomy nurse to follow up.

sections.heading: Collaborative therapies: medications and surgery
sections.body: When independent measures aren't enough, the provider may order medications. Your slides list three groups, and surgery for cases of obstruction, ulceration, perforation, or cancer. Surgery may remove part of the bowel and sometimes creates an ostomy.

table.caption: Bowel medications
rows: Laxatives (for example, bulk-forming psyllium, osmotic polyethylene glycol [Miralax], stimulant bisacodyl or senna)
Promote a bowel movement by adding bulk, drawing water into the bowel, or stimulating peristalsis

Never give with a suspected obstruction or unexplained abdominal pain. Give bulk-forming types with a full glass of water. Long-term use inhibits the bowel's natural reflexes and can cause dependence and electrolyte losses. Teach clients to avoid routine use.
Stool softeners (for example, docusate)
Let water mix into stool so it is soft and passes without straining
For clients who shouldn't strain: after surgery or childbirth, with hemorrhoids, or while taking opioids. They prevent hard stool rather than produce a quick bowel movement.
Antidiarrheal agents (for example, loperamide)
Slow intestinal movement so more water is absorbed
Check with the provider if an infectious cause is suspected, because slowing the bowel can hold the germ or its toxin inside. Watch for constipation. Keep replacing fluids.

check.q: A client with abdominal distention, vomiting, and no flatus asks for a laxative. Why should the nurse hold it and notify the provider?
check.a: These are signs of a possible bowel obstruction. Laxatives must not be given with a blockage, because they increase pressure behind it and raise the risk of perforation.

sections.heading: Bowel elimination connects to other concepts
sections.body: Your slides link bowel elimination to six other concepts. Problems in any of them can cause bowel problems, and bowel problems can cause problems in them.

table.caption: Concepts related to bowel elimination
rows: Cognition
A client with dementia or confusion may not recognize the urge or find the bathroom, which leads to incontinence or constipation.
Fluids and Electrolytes
Diarrhea removes fluid and electrolytes; low fluid intake causes hard stool.
Infection
Infections cause diarrhea; stool on the skin or near the urethra spreads infection.
Inflammation
Inflamed bowel tissue (such as diverticulitis) changes bowel function and can obstruct or perforate.
Mobility
Immobility slows peristalsis, and impaired mobility makes it hard to reach the toilet in time.
Teaching and Learning
Most prevention and self-care (diet, fluids, bowel routine, ostomy care) depends on effective teaching.

sections.heading: Prevention: healthy habits
sections.body: Your prevention slide covers both bladder and bowel health. Many of the same habits protect both.
bullets: Healthy lifestyle habits: maintain a healthy weight (extra weight presses on the pelvic floor) and exercise regularly (activity stimulates peristalsis).

Good toileting habits: avoid delaying voiding and defecation, because held stool dries out and the urge weakens over time. Avoid using the pelvic floor muscles to force urine out, because straining to push urine strains and weakens those muscles.
Adequate fluid and fiber in the diet, and a high-fiber diet in general.
Treat constipation or diarrhea as it occurs, before it leads to impaction, dehydration, or skin breakdown.
Don't smoke. Smoking is a risk factor for both urinary and fecal incontinence; chronic coughing also strains the pelvic floor.
Ensure adequate fluid intake.
Avoid foods and drinks that irritate the bladder and bowel, such as caffeine, alcohol, artificial sweeteners, and spicy or acidic foods.

sections.heading: Modifiable risk factors
sections.body: Your slides list risk factors that can be changed or reduced. Knowing why each one matters helps you target your teaching.

table.caption: Modifiable risk factors for elimination problems
rows: Obesity
Extra abdominal weight puts pressure on the bladder and pelvic floor.
Pregnancy
The growing uterus presses on the bowel and bladder, and hormones slow the bowel; childbirth can stretch or injure the pelvic floor.
Medical procedures that require anesthesia
Anesthesia slows peristalsis and can cause constipation or ileus.
Pharmacologic treatment of other conditions
Medications for other problems affect the bowel: opioids and iron constipate; antibiotics can cause diarrhea.
Lower socioeconomic status and lower education levels
Less access to healthy food, health information, and health care.
Poor hygiene
Germs spread from stool to mouth, causing infectious diarrhea.
Poor diet; poor cooking and storing of food
Low-fiber diets cause constipation; undercooked or poorly stored food causes foodborne illness.
Traveling, especially to developing countries
Exposure to unsafe water and food can cause traveler's diarrhea. Teach bottled or treated water and well-cooked food.

sections.heading: Screening: you have to ask
sections.body:
Your slides note there are no standard screening procedures for elimination problems. Instead, nurses and providers use verbal screening for abnormal symptoms during regular checkups, especially for older adults.

Elimination problems require more direct questioning than other medical problems. Clients are often embarrassed, or they assume leaking or constipation is just part of getting older, so they won't bring it up on their own. Your slides are clear: urinary incontinence and retention are never considered normal, and they often indicate another medical problem. The same is true of fecal incontinence.
sections.example: At the bedside: Instead of "Any problems?", ask directly and kindly: "Many people have trouble with leaking urine or stool, or with constipation. Do you ever leak when you cough or can't make it to the bathroom in time? How often do you have a bowel movement?" Direct, normalizing questions get honest answers.

check.q: An 80-year-old client says, "I leak a little urine now and then, but that's normal at my age." How should the nurse respond?
check.a: Explain that urinary incontinence is never considered normal and often points to another medical problem that can be treated, and report it so the provider can evaluate it.

pearls: Fluid and fiber work together. Increase fiber gradually and with fluid, and check for fluid restrictions first.
Use the gastrocolic reflex: schedule toileting after meals, sitting upright, with privacy and time.
Never give a laxative when obstruction is suspected.
Long-term laxative use inhibits the bowel's natural reflexes. Teach clients to rely on diet, fluid, and activity instead.
Empty an ostomy pouch when it is one-third to one-half full; cut the barrier to fit closely around the stoma.
Urinary incontinence and retention are never normal. Ask directly, especially older adults.
redFlags: A client asking for a laxative who has distention, vomiting, and no stool or flatus → hold the laxative and notify the provider; it may be an obstruction.
Diarrhea that continues after an antidiarrheal is started, or with fever or blood → report; there may be an infection that needs a different treatment.
Peristomal skin that is raw or open → stool is leaking onto the skin; refit the pouch and involve the wound and ostomy nurse.
recap: Independent: fluid and fiber, diet teaching, bowel training, pelvic floor exercises, personal hygiene, ostomy care.
Collaborative: laxatives, stool softeners, antidiarrheal agents; surgery for obstruction, ulceration, perforation, or cancer.
Related concepts: cognition, fluids and electrolytes, infection, inflammation, mobility, teaching and learning.
Prevention: healthy weight, exercise, don't delay voiding or defecation, don't force urine with the pelvic floor, fluid and fiber, treat constipation or diarrhea early, don't smoke, avoid irritants.
Modifiable risks: obesity, pregnancy, anesthesia, medications, lower SES and education, poor hygiene, poor diet and food handling, travel.
No standard screening exists. Ask directly during checkups, especially older adults; incontinence and retention are never normal.

checks.q: Which two independent measures are the first line for constipation, and how do they work together?
checks.a: Increased fluid and fiber. Fiber adds bulk and holds water; fluid supplies the water so stool stays soft and keeps moving.

checks.q: When is the best time of day to schedule bowel training, and why?
checks.a: After a meal, often breakfast, because eating triggers the gastrocolic reflex, which pushes stool toward the rectum.

checks.q: A post-op client taking opioids must avoid straining. Which medication group is most fitting?
checks.a: A stool softener, which keeps stool soft so it passes without straining.

checks.q: A traveler is heading to a developing country. What bowel-related teaching applies?
checks.a: Travel is a risk factor for diarrhea: drink bottled or treated water, eat well-cooked food, and wash hands.

topics.title: Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: What counts as normal bowel elimination changes with age: seedy yellow stools in a breastfed baby, toilet training in toddlers, sluggish bowels in pregnancy, and constipation in older adults. Knowing these norms helps you reassure families and catch what is truly abnormal.
objectives: After this lesson you can describe normal stool in newborns and infants and explain how breastfeeding, formula, and solid foods change it.
State the expected ages for bowel control and toilet training.
Recognize intussusception as the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3, and its warning signs.
Explain why constipation, hemorrhoids, and flatulence occur during pregnancy and after birth.
Explain why constipation is common in older adults, why laxative overuse backfires, and when a change in bowel habits should be referred.
topics.bigPicture:
The same stool that is perfectly normal in one client is worrying in another. A loose, mustard-yellow, seedy stool is normal for a breastfed baby. In an adult, the same stool would mean diarrhea. A child who isn't toilet trained at 2 is on track; a child who isn't at 5 may need evaluation.

This lesson walks through the stages of life your slides cover: newborns and infants, toddlers, school-age children and adolescents, pregnant women, and older adults. For each one, learn what is normal, what is common, and what should make you act.

keyTerms.def: A newborn's first stools: thick, sticky, and greenish-black.
A wave of colon activity triggered when food enters the stomach, often creating the urge to defecate after a meal.
A condition in which one part of the intestine slides (telescopes) into the next part, blocking it. The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3.
A pregnancy hormone that relaxes smooth muscle, including the muscle of the GI tract.
Swollen veins in the rectum or anus, made worse by pressure and straining.
Learning to control bowel and bladder and use the toilet, usually completed in the preschool years.

sections.heading: Newborns: the first stools
sections.body:
A newborn's first stools are meconium: thick, sticky, and greenish-black. Most newborns pass meconium within the first 24 hours of life. A newborn who hasn't passed any stool by about 48 hours should be reported, because it can signal a blockage or another problem. Over the next few days, as the baby feeds, stools change to lighter transitional stools and then to the normal infant stools described below.

Your slides note that in newborns and infants, frequency varies and may depend on breast or formula feeding. Breastfed babies often stool more often, sometimes after every feeding, while formula-fed babies tend to stool less often.

check.q: A newborn is 50 hours old and has not passed any stool. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Report it. Most newborns pass meconium within 24 hours; none by about 48 hours can signal a blockage or another problem.

sections.heading: Breastfed vs formula-fed stools
sections.body: Parents often worry about the color and looseness of their baby's stool. Use this table to reassure them about what is normal.

table.caption: Infant stools (from your slides)
rows: Color
Mustard yellow
Ranges from tan to yellow to green
Appearance
Seedy (small curds)
Less seedy, more pasty
Consistency
Soft and liquid
Soft and liquid (often a bit pastier)
Odor
Faint
Faint

bullets: Consistency is soft and liquid, and it becomes firmer when the infant starts solid food.
Odor is faint until the infant starts solid food. After that, stools smell more like adult stools.
Switching from breast milk to formula can change the stool's appearance.
sections.example: At the bedside: A new mother says, "My breastfed baby's diaper is full of runny yellow stuff with little seeds in it. Does she have diarrhea?" You can reassure her that mustard-yellow, seedy, loose stools are normal for a breastfed infant. Then teach what would be worrying: very watery stools much more often than usual, blood in the stool, or signs of dehydration such as fewer wet diapers, a dry mouth, or a sunken soft spot (fontanel).

check.q: A formula-fed infant has a green, pasty stool. Is this abnormal?
check.a: No. Formula-fed stools normally range from tan to yellow to green.

sections.heading: Toddlers: gaining control
sections.body: Your slides give two key ages:
bullets: Some bowel control between 1.5 and 2 years of age (18–24 months), as the nerves and muscles that control the anal sphincter mature.
Successful toilet training by 36 to 48 months of age (3 to 4 years).
steps: Watch for readiness signs: the child can walk to the toilet, sit, pull pants down, stay dry for a couple of hours, show interest, and tell a parent they need to go.
Use a regular routine, such as sitting on the potty after meals to use the gastrocolic reflex.
Praise success and never punish accidents. Punishment and pressure can lead a child to hold stool, which causes constipation.
Expect setbacks during stress, such as a new sibling, a move, or illness.
sections.analogy: Toilet training is like learning to ride a bike. The child has to be physically ready (balance, leg strength) before practice works, and there will be some falls along the way.

sections.heading: Intussusception: an emergency in young children
sections.body:
Your slides state that intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3 years old. In intussusception, one section of intestine slides inside the next section, the way a telescope folds into itself. This is a mechanical obstruction: stool can't pass, and the folded bowel's blood supply gets squeezed. Without treatment, the bowel tissue can die and perforate.

Know the classic warning signs:
bullets: Sudden, severe, crampy abdominal pain that comes in waves. The child screams and draws the knees up to the chest, then may seem calm or sleepy between episodes.
Vomiting.
"Currant jelly" stools: stool mixed with blood and mucus. This is usually a later sign.
Sometimes a sausage-shaped lump can be felt in the abdomen.
sections.analogy: Picture pulling off a sock by rolling it down so it folds inside itself. The rolled part gets thick and tight. That is what happens to the bowel in intussusception, and the tight fold pinches off its blood supply.
sections.example: At the bedside: A parent brings in a 10-month-old who keeps screaming and pulling his legs up, vomited twice, and now has a red, jelly-like stool in the diaper. These are classic signs of intussusception. Notify the provider immediately. This is an emergency that needs prompt diagnosis and treatment.

check.q: What is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3?
check.a: Intussusception, when one part of the intestine telescopes into the next.

sections.heading: School-age children and adolescents
sections.body:
Your slides note that by school age, bowel habits are similar to adults', and frequency, quantity, and consistency vary from child to child.

The same risk factors that affect adults start to show up. Busy school days, embarrassment about using school bathrooms, and being "too busy" to stop playing can lead children to hold stool, which leads to constipation. Diets high in fast food and low in fruits, vegetables, and water add to the problem. Teach children and families about fiber, fluids, activity, and not ignoring the urge to go.

check.q: A 9-year-old has hard stools and says he never uses the school bathroom. What is the likely link?
check.a: Holding stool lets it dry out and harden, causing constipation. Teach not to ignore the urge, plus fiber, fluids, and activity.

sections.heading: Pregnancy and after birth
sections.body: Pregnancy changes the bowel in predictable ways. Your slides explain the chain of events:
steps: Elevated progesterone relaxes smooth muscle throughout the body, including the GI tract.
This causes delayed gastric emptying and decreased peristalsis, so food and stool move more slowly.
Slower movement gives the colon more time to absorb water, which may lead to bloating and constipation.
As the uterus enlarges, it crowds and presses on the intestines, which aggravates these symptoms. Iron in prenatal vitamins can add to constipation.
Late in pregnancy, pressure on the rectal veins plus straining with hard stool leads to hemorrhoids.
bullets: Bowels are sluggish after giving birth. Labor, decreased food intake, and stretched abdominal muscles all slow things down.

Pain may lead to delaying elimination. A sore perineum, stitches, or hemorrhoids make the new mother afraid to have a bowel movement. Delay lets stool harden, which makes the next BM even more painful.
Flatulence after cesarean birth: abdominal surgery and anesthesia slow peristalsis, so gas builds up and causes painful bloating.
sections.example: At the bedside: On the first day after birth, a client with a perineal tear says she is afraid to have a bowel movement. You give the pain medication as ordered, encourage fluids, fiber, and walking, give the stool softener if ordered, and explain that keeping stool soft will make the first bowel movement less painful. For a client after a cesarean birth with gas pain, early and frequent walking helps most.

sections.heading: Older adults: constipation is common
sections.body: Your slides state that constipation is common in older adults and list four main reasons:

table.caption: Why older adults become constipated
rows: Reduced activity levels
Less movement means slower peristalsis.
Encourage walking and activity as tolerated.
Inadequate fluid and fiber intake
Reduced thirst, limiting fluids to avoid incontinence, dental problems that make fruits and vegetables hard to chew, and less access to fresh food.
Offer fluids regularly through the day; suggest soft high-fiber foods (cooked vegetables, oatmeal, prunes).
Muscle weakness
Weaker abdominal and pelvic muscles make it harder to push stool out.
Use an upright, supported position on the toilet; encourage activity.
Medication side effects
Older adults often take many medications; opioids, iron, and others slow the bowel.
Review the medication list and report drugs that may be contributing.

bullets: Responding to the gastrocolic reflex is important. Help the client to the toilet after meals, especially breakfast, and answer call lights quickly so the urge isn't lost.
Laxative use inhibits natural reflexes and may cause constipation rather than relieve it. The bowel comes to depend on the laxative, so the client takes more, and the cycle continues.

EDUCATE! Teach fluids, fiber, activity, and a regular routine instead of daily laxatives. Many older adults believe they must have a bowel movement every day. Explain that a normal range varies and that every day is not required.

check.q: An older adult takes a stimulant laxative every night "to stay regular" and says it isn't working as well. What is happening?
check.a: Routine laxative use inhibits the bowel's natural reflexes, so the bowel becomes dependent and constipation can actually get worse. Teach fluid, fiber, activity, and toileting after meals, and report the laxative use to the provider.

sections.heading: When a change is a warning sign
sections.body:
Your slides give one more key rule for older adults: a change in bowel habits over weeks should be referred to the primary care provider. A lasting change, such as new constipation, new diarrhea, narrower stools, or blood in the stool, can be an early sign of a serious problem such as colorectal cancer, whose risk rises with age. Don't let the client or family write it off as "just getting older."

The same goes for bowel incontinence. Like urinary incontinence, it is not a normal part of aging. It usually signals another problem that can often be treated.
sections.example: At the bedside: A 74-year-old client mentions that for the past month her stools have been thinner and she has had constipation alternating with loose stools. She shrugs it off as age. Encourage her to see her primary care provider soon, and document and report the finding.

pearls: Mustard-yellow, seedy, loose stool is normal for a breastfed baby. Formula-fed stool ranges from tan to yellow to green.
Infant stools get firmer and smell stronger once solid foods begin.
Some bowel control at 1.5–2 years; successful toilet training by 36–48 months.
Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction under age 3: severe intermittent pain with knees to chest, vomiting, and currant-jelly stool.
Pregnancy: progesterone slows the gut, and the growing uterus makes it worse. Expect constipation, bloating, and late hemorrhoids.
Older adults: laxative overuse can cause constipation. Educate, and refer any change in bowel habits lasting weeks.
redFlags: An infant or toddler with episodes of severe crying and knees drawn to the chest, vomiting, and red jelly-like stool → suspect intussusception; notify the provider immediately.
A newborn who hasn't passed meconium by about 48 hours → report; it may indicate an obstruction.
An older adult with a change in bowel habits lasting weeks (new constipation, diarrhea, thin stools, or blood) → refer to the primary care provider.
recap: Newborn and infant stool frequency varies and depends on breast or formula feeding.
Breastfed: mustard yellow and seedy. Formula-fed: tan to yellow to green. Soft and liquid, firmer with solids. Odor faint until solids.
Toddlers: some control at 1.5–2 years; trained by 36–48 months.
Intussusception: most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3.
School-age and adolescents: habits similar to adults; frequency, quantity, and consistency vary.
Pregnancy: progesterone → delayed gastric emptying and less peristalsis → bloating and constipation; the uterus aggravates it; hemorrhoids late.
After birth: sluggish bowels; pain delays elimination; flatulence after cesarean.

Older adults: constipation is common (reduced activity, low fluid and fiber, muscle weakness, medications); respond to the gastrocolic reflex; laxatives can backfire; educate; refer changes lasting weeks.

checks.q: Why does constipation commonly occur in pregnancy? Give two reasons from your slides.
checks.a: Elevated progesterone delays gastric emptying and decreases peristalsis, and the enlarging uterus presses on the intestines and aggravates the symptoms.

checks.q: A mother says her 6-month-old's stools became firmer and smellier after she started rice cereal and pureed vegetables. Is this expected?
checks.a: Yes. Infant stool becomes firmer and its odor stronger once solid foods are started.

checks.q: Why might a postpartum client become constipated even if she was regular during pregnancy?
checks.a: The bowels are sluggish after birth, and pain from a tear, stitches, or hemorrhoids can make her delay elimination, which lets stool harden.

checks.q: Which nursing action best uses the gastrocolic reflex for an older adult with constipation?
checks.a: Helping the client to the toilet shortly after meals, especially breakfast, and responding promptly to the urge.
